Did scarcity make old media (VHS, disc/cartridge games...) easier to enjoy?

Interesting question. I'll stick to video games because I that's a clearer picture whereas the movie debate is largely one of cultural preference (old people like old movies as cultural norms are closer to theirs and they remember the shared experience). I think there are two angles here worth considering. The first is novelty and the second is market share. Indulge me here because it's a complicated question without a clear answer although the two do tie together.

In terms of novelty its a two way street. There is no doubt that games like Mario and Sonic where novelties in a way that we haven't seen in some time. Although games are certainly more technologically sophisticated now the difference between systems is linearly larger but from an experiential point of view a PS4 is essentially a PS3 with better graphics with some hardware differences that are largely invisible to the end user. Whereas the difference between a N64/PS1 and SNES was truly revolutionary similar to the gap between the ataris and nintendo. So from an enjoy-ability standpoint the older systems had a much larger relative edge in terms of technological innovation IMO. This also created a much larger sense of shared cultural experience due to the shear novelty. The advent of online gaming should also be considered here as a tremendous detriment to social gaming (gaming with real life friends during a lan party is way better than online gaming even with the same friends in party IMO).

As far as scarcity there are a couple ways to think about this. The first is driven by novelty. Today you could easily live your life a couple years behind the gaming crowd and be none the worse for it particularly if online gaming isn't something you enjoy. A PS3 is in many regards every bit as enjoyable as a PS4 particularly when you factor in game cost. We have an over abundance of enjoyable games which erodes the shared cultural experience (seriously no one cares if you play COD it isn't the same cultural phenomenon that say Mortal Kombat was). With fewer AAA franchises the console companies had to push to create truly memorable games to create market share after the Ataris video game collapse (look it up video games weren't popular in America again as an adult hobby for a decade or two). This lead to the rise of console selling franchises mario, zelda, sonic, Resident evil, madden etc. Each of these franchises developed loyal followings behind a shared cultural experience that is in many ways unmatched today in part due to scarcity and in part due to the large gap in functionality between the early systems. That being said there were plenty of shit games back then too but we do tend to selectively forget those. In some regards the games were better from a story telling standpoint. The studio had to work a lot harder to establish these franchises than they do to keep them alive today (not a knock on any specific game but some of the annual release games are ridiculous. Seriously how often do you really need to upgrade madden). Add onto that the tech leap and you have a recipe for a golden age of gaming.
It's just your age. When you're a kid you're less worried about shit, and everything's new to you. You can fully enjoy something without any baggage.
I never bought a game cartridge I didn't damn near wear out, but I've pirated games I've yet to play.
